# 14. Working with an AI agent (MCP)

Every project has an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server (`<game>_mcp` from the checkout build, or
the stock `mce_mcp --module <lib<game>.so>`, `mce mcp` with the SDK) that gives an AI agent
the same scene-editing commands a person has in the editor, plus cook and headless verification.
Three games in the repository were authored entirely this way (Kindle's level, Prism Break and
Undertow), and a fourth (Lamplighter) by an agent that had never seen the engine source. This
chapter is the workflow that worked and the pitfalls it found.

## 14.1 Starting the server

```sh
build/<preset>/projects/MyGame/my_game_mcp --project projects/MyGame
build/<preset>/projects/MyGame/my_game_mcp --project projects/MyGame --scene scenes/main.mcscene
build/<preset>/projects/MyGame/my_game_mcp --project projects/MyGame --allow-cheats
build/<preset>/src/editor/mcp/mce_mcp --module build/<preset>/projects/MyGame/libmy_game.so --project projects/MyGame
mce mcp MyGame                                      # the SDK: the line above with its own paths
```

The server speaks JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdin and stdout, one message per line (the MCP stdio
transport); it opens no socket. Stdout carries nothing else: logs go to stderr, and so does the
command line `mce mcp` prints before it starts the server. Use the **project's** server or the stock one **with the module**:

# 8. 3D games

A 3D game is a scene of **kit3d components** plus a game module, played by the stock player, the
same way a 2D game is a scene of 2D kit components (chapter 7). The scene places models, lights, a
camera, the sky and static colliders; the module's systems move things and drive the camera; the
player draws it all with the physically based forward renderer (cascaded shadows, Forward+ point
and spot lights, sky, fog, bloom, tonemap, FXAA) and runs it headless, with `-capture_tick`,
`-input` scripts and `-save` slots like any other game. The editor viewport shows the same scene.

`projects/Room3D` is the small reference (`mce example Room3D` copies it out of the SDK) and
`projects/SolsticeReach` the large one: an island with a time of day, scatter, beams and a HUD,
all from a module on the kit. A program that owns its renderer (`samples/04_cubes`,
`05_ashen_court`) still works and is covered at the end of the chapter.

## 8.1 A 3D scene on the kit

The components live in `mce/kit/kit3d.h`; the editor's inspector, the cook and the MCP server know
them. Conventions: right-handed, Y up, metres; an entity's `LocalTransform` places it (its
`WorldTransform` when it has a parent), and cameras look down their local −Z.

# 10. Audio

Audio is a 48 kHz stereo float mixer on its own thread with 48 real voices, buses with EQ and a
limiter, sample-accurate scheduling and 3D attenuation. From a game you touch it in three ways: an
`AudioSource` component for sounds that belong to an entity, a `PlaySfx` event for one-shots, and
convars for the bus volumes.

## 10.1 Sounds that belong to an entity

```json
"Torch": {
  "LocalTransform": { "position": [4, 1, 0] },
  "AudioSource": { "clip": "guid:<crackle.wav>", "loop": true, "play_on_start": true, "gain_db": -6 }
}
```

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `clip` | the `.wav` asset |
| `gain_db`, `pan` | −60..12 dB, −1..1 |
| `priority` | 0..255; louder and higher priority voices survive when voices run out |
| `bus` | `Master`, `Music`, `SFX` (default) or `UI` (`audio::AudioBus`; scenes written with the number, `"bus": 1`, still load). `Music` streams the clip in 100 ms pages instead of holding it decoded (two music streams at a time; a third plays from memory) |
| `loop` | gapless; the clip's loop points come from the WAV's own markers or the sidecar's `loop_start` / `loop_end` |
| `play_on_start` | start when the entity appears |
| `fade_s` | seconds the voice fades in when it starts and out when the component or entity is removed |

Changing `gain_db` or `pan` from code ramps over 10 ms (no clicks). Removing the component stops

# 14. Working with an AI agent (MCP)

Every project has an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server (`<game>_mcp` from the checkout build, or
the stock `mce_mcp --module <lib<game>.so>`, `mce mcp` with the SDK) that gives an AI agent
the same scene-editing commands a person has in the editor, plus cook and headless verification.
Three games in the repository were authored entirely this way (Kindle's level, Prism Break and
Undertow), and a fourth (Lamplighter) by an agent that had never seen the engine source. This
chapter is the workflow that worked and the pitfalls it found.

## 14.1 Starting the server

```sh
build/<preset>/projects/MyGame/my_game_mcp --project projects/MyGame
build/<preset>/projects/MyGame/my_game_mcp --project projects/MyGame --scene scenes/main.mcscene
build/<preset>/projects/MyGame/my_game_mcp --project projects/MyGame --allow-cheats
build/<preset>/src/editor/mcp/mce_mcp --module build/<preset>/projects/MyGame/libmy_game.so --project projects/MyGame
mce mcp MyGame                                      # the SDK: the line above with its own paths
```

The server speaks JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdin and stdout, one message per line (the MCP stdio
transport); it opens no socket. Stdout carries nothing else: logs go to stderr, and so does the
command line `mce mcp` prints before it starts the server. Use the **project's** server or the stock one **with the module**:
without `--module`, `mce_mcp` knows only the engine's components (the visual-novel kit's included) and r [... 29022 characters cut]

# Screens that stay right

You want to know when a change breaks how a screen looks, without a person looking.

1. **Get it right once.** `render_frame {"tick": 30}` (and with `input` to reach a moment, e.g.
   `"1-90 Move=1,0"`) until the screen looks as intended. A phone layout:
   `"safe_area": {"top": 48, "bottom": 34}`.
2. **Bless it.** `image_diff {"golden": "goldens/title.png", "render": {"tick": 30}}`: with no golden
   yet, the frame becomes the golden. Do the same for each level's first frame.
3. **Check after every change.** The same call returns `score` (0 is identical), `changed_fraction`
   and `pass` (`score <= max_score`, default 0.01), with a heat map image of what moved. A failing
   score on a screen you did not mean to change is a regression; on one you did, look at the frame
   and pass `update: true` to bless it again.
4. **Several moments at once.** `render_sheet {"ticks": [1, 60, 120, 240], "cameras": [{}, {"center": [12, 3], "zoom": 0.5}]}`
   gives one image to review.

Frames come from the real player (offscreen software rendering without a display), so the same
arguments give the same pixels on the same machine. Keep goldens in the project (they are PNG files
under any folder you choose) and commit them with the scenes.
